50.chaz:
I loved Chainsaw Man for its raw action scenes and "heavy metal" themes. I relate to Denji as a hopeless romantic who takes life as it comes and doesn't read too much into expectations. I did not expect the anime to hit so deep once the Reze arc began. That's when I knew it was something far beyond another Shonen Jump monster-of-the-week action show.

Reze and Denji's story, not giving up on someone you care about no matter how much they push back, forgiving their lies once the truth comes out, goofy friends like Power who show up when you need them, and some of the tragedy itself are all things I've experienced. An anime that is so relatable, even to some of your worst moments in life, breathes real life into a simple work of fiction. There's something special in a piece of art that reminds you of your harshest struggles and somehow paints them as beautiful moments instead of reminders of pain. How this show did that, I'm still not sure. Even though it made me cry, it reminded me of the things I'm proud I did, even if I don't have much to show for them. Maybe that comes from watching someone else do it instead of doing it myself (apart from riding sharks with chains). Either way, for me it felt healing.
50.frost: The story is fantastic with a great love story and at the same time a tragedy,  but one done in such a beautiful way. Reze starts out with deceit while Denji feels hopelessly taken with her. In the end, even with the truth laid bare, Denji can't find it in himself to kill her and she can't find it in herself to leave him forever. Beautiful animation sequences for things as simple as their pool scene. Incredible perspective, camera angles, and action shots, a definitive work of art on every level.

4.chaz:
First I'll say this: if Perfect Blue meets Detective Conan sounds good to you, you're already sold. This is another one that hits really close to home, though. A person who is a big part of my life was also left to be raised by others and never really shown what love was, but was then expected to somehow show it to others. Ai keeping a brave face and moving forward is the kind of courage I always see in this person, and I hope anyone who sees it is inspired. That part is just as real as the pitfalls of fame in the show.

It's also a painfully accurate portrayal of those pitfalls. In my own life I've experienced the dangers of meeting fans, fans breaking into my private life, stealing pictures, insulting me and my loved ones, demanding I keep entertaining them, and calling me washed up when I couldn't. But at the same time there's the reward of giving thousands of people joy, and the memories of each person you did something for, even if they think you don't remember. My run in entertainment was maybe a tiny fraction of the level you see in this show, but it's all very real. For anyone considering entertainment, it's probably a really good show to watch for both the rewards and the pitfalls. As for me, I'm just glad I'm mostly forgotten and can relive it from the audience's perspective, even if part of me still misses it.

9.frost:
Haikyuu!! is about chasing dreams and the joy of aspirations. Every character here knows they're not the best but wants to be the best. And unlike the super-ego approach of Blue Lock, the attitude here is "I'm going to be the best, but I cannot carry this entire team on my back. There are things I cannot do that others can, and I'll bring those people with me. We are all taking that step forward, together." It's a beautiful message and teamwork oriented.

At the same time each character has a background where they just want to play the game. They've spent years honing their craft and you get to see it. The characters develop from the beginning without skills instead of having some fully formed innate talent from the get go. They're always learning new tricks, always evolving, and always learning to trust someone. Unlike most wish fulfillment Anime, this one shows how important trust building is and what real teamwork looks like.

I've played soccer for two and a half years and martial arts for seven years, but when I watch sports anime I just feel like part of the crowd. I'm an enjoyer of sports as an audience member and a fan as I watch these people keep developing. This is one of the best at capturing that feeling, and it has me as a fan going, "OH MY GOD, OH MY GOD!"

23.chaz:
If you're a fan of this genre, I'd probably recommend the manga more, since it has the full ending. Either way, the manga's production value is good quality and anime while not as big as others still pulls through. Much like Ranma ½, it explores discovering feelings for someone, and something in yourself that you may or may not understand yet.

My own discovery was much like the show's: feeling confident in myself until one day I discovered a feeling that seemed like something I shouldn't feel. Then came the fear of exploring a part of yourself that society doesn't really give you a rulebook for.

The main character's mistakes are really punished by the critics, though I think that's just them trying to find something wrong with material they already don't like. The characters aren't perfect, and they're very confused. Watching them slowly discover themselves is the entire LGBTQ experience. All the exciting, confused and doubtful moments I fully related with and capture it all for me. I enjoyed it until the end.
